title: Building hollow clay forms without cracking
subtitle: How to maintain even wall thickness and control drying to prevent cracks in sculptural pieces
excerpt: Hollow air-dry clay forms crack when one wall is thicker than another, or when the clay dries unevenly. The technique for preventing this starts at the forming stage and continues through the drying stage. Even walls, matched moisture levels, and slow drying are the three controls.
sourceNotes: Hollow form construction and crack prevention derived from first principles.

glossaryTerms.definition: The stage at which clay holds its shape firmly; the best time to check and correct wall thickness

content.text: Hollow
greenware

cracks when different sections of the piece dry at different rates. A thick wall shrinks less than a thin wall. Where the two meet, the thinner section pulls away as it shrinks and a crack forms at the join. Even walls and slow, even drying are the primary controls.
Why hollow forms crack

Air-dry clay shrinks as water evaporates. If a thick section and a thin section next to it shrink at the same rate, the relative movement is small and the join holds. If the thinner section shrinks faster, it pulls against the thicker section and the clay splits at the transition. The more dramatic the wall thickness difference, the more likely the crack.
What you need
Air-dry clay piece in progress, at any hand-building stage
Wooden rib for smoothing and compressing
Needle tool for checking wall thickness
Loose cloth or polythene bag for drying rate control
Step-by-step

While forming, check wall thickness at every stage by pressing a needle tool horizontally through the wall at several points. The needle leaves a mark at the entry point; pull it out and measure how far the tip has penetrated. Aim for 6-8 mm for most hand-built hollow forms.
After forming, compress all surfaces with a wooden rib, working in firm smooth strokes. Compression closes surface pores and aligns the clay particles, which reduces cracking tendency during drying.
Check joins between attached pieces (handles, spouts, coils) and ensure they are the same thickness as the surrounding wall. A thick join on a thin-walled pot is a common crack site.

Slow the drying rate. Cover the piece loosely with a cloth or inside a loose polythene bag. The cover traps humidity around the piece, slowing evaporation and allowing all sections to dry at the same rate. Do not seal airtight; the piece needs to breathe.
At leather-hard stage, check all join lines and any changes in wall section. Dampen and blend any hairline cracks before they widen.
Remove the cover gradually over the last 12-24 hours of drying. Bringing the piece out of the covered environment slowly prevents a rapid humidity change that can crack a nearly-dry surface.
Allow to reach bone-dry before moving or sealing.
What correct drying looks like
A piece drying without cracking stays the same colour throughout, with no darker areas at the base or on one side. Uneven colour means uneven moisture. At
leather-hard
the whole piece should feel the same firmness throughout. At
bone-dry
the piece is pale, evenly lightweight, and shows no crack lines.
Common mistakes
Drying in direct sun or near a radiator. Fast surface drying creates a hard crust while the interior is still wet; the interior then cracks through the crust as it shrinks.
Drying a piece flat on a non-porous surface. The base cannot breathe and dries slower than the sides, warping or cracking the base.
Repairing a crack at bone-dry with fresh clay. Fresh wet clay shrinks; bone-dry clay does not. The patch will crack again. Use PVA adhesive for bone-dry repairs.
